:::{#def-mixed-model}
#### Mixed-effects model

A **mixed-effects model** (or **mixed model**)
is a regression model that contains
both fixed effects (@def-fixed-effect)
and random effects (@def-random-effect)
[@rocke2021epi204; @dobson4e, Chapter 11].
For example, a linear mixed model with a random intercept for each group is
$$
Y_{ij} \eqdef \tp{\vx_{ij}}\vb + \alpha_i + \epsilon_{ij},
$$
where $\vb$ is a vector of fixed effects,
$\alpha_i \siid \ndist{0, \sigma_\alpha^2}$ is the random effect of group $i$,
and $\epsilon_{ij} \siid \ndist{0, \sigma^2}$ is independent of the $\alpha_i$s.
:::

::: notes
Whether a term is fixed or random is part of the *model structure*.
It does not determine the *inference method*:
the same mixed-effects model can be fit by maximum likelihood,
by restricted maximum likelihood (REML),
or by Bayesian inference.
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-mixed-model}
#### Drug trial with repeated measurements

Combining @exm-fixed-effect and @exm-random-effect,
suppose that each patient in the drug trial has blood pressure measured several times,
and that
$$
Y_{ij} = \b_0 + \b_1 x_{ij} + \alpha_i + \epsilon_{ij},
$$
with fixed effects $\b_0 = 120$ and $\b_1 = -8$,
and patient random effects $\alpha_i \siid \ndist{0, 10^2}$.
If patient 3 takes the drug ($x_{3j} = 1$)
and that patient's random effect is $\alpha_3 = 7$,
then the mean blood pressure of patient 3 is:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\E{Y_{3j}|x_{3j} = 1, \alpha_3 = 7}
&= \b_0 + \b_1 \cdot 1 + \alpha_3
&& \text{(substitute $x_{3j} = 1$; $\E{\epsilon_{3j}} = 0$)}\\
&= 120 + (-8) \cdot 1 + 7
&& \text{(substitute the values)}\\
&= 119
&& \text{(arithmetic)}
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-not-mixed-model}
#### A model with only fixed effects

The model in @exm-fixed-effect is not a mixed-effects model:
both of its coefficients are fixed effects,
and it has no random effects.
:::
